title: Hubble eXtreme Deep Field (XDF)
caption: The Hubble eXtreme Deep Field, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: Hubble eXtreme Deep Field, XDF · constellation Fornax
credit: NASA, ESA, G. Illingworth, D. Magee, and P. Oesch (University of California, Santa Cruz), R. Bouwens (Leiden University), and the HUDF09 Team

recognition.text: NASA Hubble image release (STScI). No published audience rating.

story: About 5,500 galaxies crowd this tiny patch of sky in the constellation Fornax, a small fraction of the full Moon's width. Spirals shaped like our Milky Way and the Andromeda galaxy sit among large, fuzzy red galaxies that have stopped forming stars, and tiny, faint, more distant galaxies are scattered across the field.

This is the eXtreme Deep Field, or XDF, made by combining 10 years of Hubble photographs of the center of the earlier Hubble Ultra Deep Field. More than 2,000 images from the Advanced Camera for Surveys and from Wide Field Camera 3, which carries Hubble's sight into the near-infrared, went into it. The faintest galaxies are one ten-billionth as bright as the eye can detect.

The red galaxies are remnants of collisions between galaxies, now in decline. The faint specks were like seedlings for today's big galaxies. Most XDF galaxies are seen while young, small and growing, often through violent mergers, and the light from some has traveled for 13.2 billion years.

understand.summary: Combines visible light from the Advanced Camera for Surveys with near-infrared light from Wide Field Camera 3. ACS F435W and F606W are shown in blue, F775W, F814W and F850LP in green, and WFC3 F105W, F125W and F160W in red.
understand.eye: Hubble returned to this patch over many visits for a total exposure of 2 million seconds, gathering light from galaxies far too faint for any eye, much of it in infrared light the eye cannot see.

explore: Its youngest galaxy dates from just 450 million years after the big bang. In 2012 astronomers expected NASA's planned James Webb Space Telescope to be aimed at the field, since its infrared vision suits light from the distant past that has been stretched to longer wavelengths by the expansion of the universe.
